Sample text:
---
# What Maps Leave Out

Every map is an act of disciplined neglect. A subway diagram shows you that Station A connects to Station B, and it drops nearly everything else: the distance between them, the hills, the river you cross, the fact that two stops that look adjacent are a forty-minute walk apart. It's a lie that makes you more useful. You get where you're going because someone decided what didn't matter.

I find this both admirable and a little unnerving, because the same principle governs almost everything we know. A biography is a map of a person. A history book is a map of a century. A memory is a map of an afternoon, and it gets redrawn a little every time you consult it, like a cartographer who can't stop fiddling.

The old European maps had their sea monsters and blank spaces, and we tend to smile at them, as if the mapmakers were naive. But the blank space was the honest part. It said: *nobody I trust has been here.* The modern failure is the opposite one, where the map is so smooth and confident that you forget it's a map. The blue dot moves along the blue line, and the world feels solved. Then the road is closed, or the bridge is out, or the "shortcut" leads into a field, and you feel a flash of betrayal, as though the territory had broken a promise.

The territory never promised anything. That's the mistake worth catching in yourself: the moment you start being annoyed at reality for not matching the diagram. It happens with people, too. We build a quick sketch of a coworker, a parent, a rival, and then feel wronged when they act off-map. *He's not like that.* Well, he is, apparently, and also like a thousand other things your sketch left out.

The best mapmakers I can imagine are the ones who know exactly what their maps are for. A hiking map exaggerates the trail, because the trail is what you'll need. A nautical chart obsesses over depth, because the sea floor is what will kill you. Neither is trying to be the world. Each is trying to answer a question, and its beauty comes from how ruthlessly it refuses to answer any other.

So maybe the practical wisdom is a pair of habits. Before trusting a map, ask what it was made for. And when the ground disagrees with the paper, believe the ground, and be a little delighted, because that mismatch is the exact place where you're about to learn something the mapmaker didn't have room for.

I like to imagine, somewhere, a map at true scale: one mile to one mile, every blade of grass included. Borges wrote about it, and it's useless, of course. It ends up rotting in a desert, tattered, inhabited by beggars and animals. That's the joke, and also the point. The value of understanding anything comes from what you're willing to throw away, as long as you remember, always, that you threw something away.
---

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW — A polished meditation with a distinctive central metaphor and a quietly personal, reflective voice.

## Grounded reading
The voice is lucid and wry, turning an everyday subway diagram into a way to think about knowledge, memory, and how we misread other people. Its pathos is mild but real: the unease of relying on simplified accounts, and the flash of betrayal when reality refuses to match them. The piece invites the reader to treat their own sketches as useful but partial—to ask what a map was made for, and to welcome the ground that exceeds it.

## What the model chose to foreground
The sample foregrounds maps, blank spaces, blue-dot navigation, and the gap between a diagram and its territory. It makes a moral claim for humility: simplification is necessary, but we should remember what it leaves out and revise our assumptions when reality disagrees. Its mood is thoughtful, lightly amused, and appreciative of surprise.
